ASUCLA, the Registration Fee Committee and Chancellor Charles E. Young, have agreed on a plan to end the campus child care program by Dec. 31, 1975. This probably will close the stormy history of the Child Care Center, which, during its five-year history, has been plagued by financial troubles.

The plan, an equal tripartite funding plan to finance the closing of the Center, was proposed by Young last Thursday and agreed to by ASUCLA's Board of Control (BOC) during its regular meeting that same day. Each will allocate $25,000 for the last months of the Center's existance. The Center was tranferred from ASUCLA ownership to the University for $14,688 during the same meeting.

The plan has the endorsement of Interim Child Care Center Director Luke Fishburn, since there is a provision to form an alternative off-campus, part-time program.

Private homes

This program, in which the children would be placed in private homes, was first suggested and rejected as part of a proposal made to Reg Fees two weeks ago by the Child Care Advisory Committee (CCAC). As part of this new proposal, it would begin as the on-campus program ends, retaining some of the personnel from the center.

While Fishburn had earlier expressed doubt as to the workability of one program starting as the other ends, the stand of both the Reg Fee Committee and Young made such a compromise inevitable. A further advantage of this plan will be the retention of a federal grant for child care which may have been lost otherwise.

Presently, the Child Care Center has facilities for 70 children at a cost of approximately $4,000 per child per year. The off campus program has a tentative beginning capacity of between 150 and 300 at a cost of about $400 per child per year.

Non professionals

However, skepticism was voiced by members of BOC and CCAC during the meeting, over the feasibility of such a program. Harold Kassarjian, faculty representative on BOC, objected to the expense of such a program. On the other hand, Dr. Patricia Greenfield, member of CCAC, objected to the program because it would provide for minimal child care in the hands of nonprofessionals.

"They're talking about expense, not quality," Greenfield said, noting that while the program may be workable for very young children, it would not give the needed stimulation to older children.

After lengthy debate, BOC passed a motion that ratified the proposal, reaffirming ASUCLA's interest in continuation of campus child care. Also, the motion was so worded that ASUCLA's commitment may not materialize at all. The $25,000 will be allocated out of "available net income." As a result of the net loss projected for this year resulting from an inventory shrinkage problem in the Student Store, there may not be any money to allocate.

Cost of living In addition to the child care issue, BOC took action in several other areas. The Board allocated over $35,000 in the form of a retroacive cost of living pay increase for ASUCLA employees. The increase was first approved in July, 1973 but help up by a Cost of Living Council ruling. Then, when the Cost of Living Council ceased to exist in April, 1974, the increase was again delayed by an injunction filed by the federal government to stop such payments. Finally, after a Supreme Court ruling last June, ASUCLA will be able to go ahead with the payment.

The BOC also approved a $400 bonus payment to each of approximately 77 ASUCLA clerical and food workers. The payment was mandated by the State Legislature and will come to a total of $30,800.

C128-01:
RSB and child care

by Gary von Ever

(Editor's note: Von Euer is a member of the Revolutionary Student Brigade).

 In the course of leafleting and circulating petitions in support of on-campus childcare, it has become apparent to us that the vast majority of members of the UCLA community are in full support of expanding the existing facilities, and have rejected the Chancellor's "outreach program" as a swindle.

We recognize that childcare is a right, not a privilege, and that if any progress is to be made in bringing more women and minority group people into the university, adequate childcare will be essential. We believe that childcare should be stimulating and educational, and not consist merely of babysitting provided by exploited custodians. We reject the idea that it is just to pay caretakers only $1.65 per hour to watch our children, and see the administration's argument that these women would stay at home unemployed otherwise as unadulterated apologetic and chauvinistic garbage. And we insist that students and workers on this campus must have the right to determine how dollars shall be spent, and whether it is really more in their interest to have an oversized department store and new alumni center to bring the big U, more $ to perpetuate the same system of priorities, or to have adequate childcare facilities for all those who need them.

We do not feel that it is our responsibility to manage the university's budget and we have no interest in the tidy separation of committees and monies which leaves childcare a mere pittance. At a time when the intensified general crisis of the monopoly capitalist system is hitting the universities in terms of cuts in financial aid, minority recruitment and tutoring programs, cuts in student health service, and the like, we must take the stand that inasmuch as we did not create this crisis, neither will we foot the bill. On the other hand, we know that there are a number of ways in which childcare could be operated in a more efficient and inexpensive manner. But university administrators are paid handsome salaries to think up such things, and so far they have only been able to repeat the old nursery rhymes about what is "cost-effective" (remember how this argument was dredged up to justify UC investments in South Africa?) and about how everyone can find childcare in the "private sector" and ought to expect that paying a fancy fee for babysitting is necessary for those who want to attend, or have the privilege of working at, UCLA.

Our task is not to help the administrators cut up their fiscal pie, but to demand what is rightfully ours: an expansion of both part- and full-time on-campus facilities to meet the needs of all students, faculty and staff.

C038-01:
In defense of Childcare

By Sally Armstrong

(Editor's note: Armstrong is a member of the Young Socialist Alliance).

The future of the child care center is in doubt. Members of the UCLA administration who sit on the University Policies Commission, the Registration Fee Committee, and the Campus Child Care Policy Advisory Committee are spearheading an attack on the present child care center.

The debate over child care has been going on for five years. As Daily Bruin writer Eric Mandel pointed out in his story of September 29th, "The concept of on-campus child care started in 1970 with a two and a half week 'baby-in' in the women's lounge of Ackerman Union."

As a result of the publicity and support generated by this demonstration, early in 1971 the child care center was established as a pilot program. Since then, the administration has attempted to undercut the effectiveness of the center.

The key issues at the present time are to defend the existing child care center and stop the center's foes from cutting back services and terminating current staff members. This requires an educational campaign to show how the administration's proposed "outreach" program—a system of farming-out children to private homes—will fail to provide care for even as many children as the existing center.

According to Bruin writer Mandel, "outreach" advocates originally projected that between 600 and 1,200 children could be cared for under their program. However, as Mandel points out, their most recent report projects that by December 1976, after a year of operation, "a minimum of 75 to 100 children will be served." This number represents no increase in children served over the existing center. In addition, the "outreach" program does not and cannot guarantee high quality care.

There is general agreement among all participants in the child care debate that the campus center does not serve enough children. But this fact is not the fault of the existing center, its staff, or the parents who have been fortunate enough to obtain on-campus child care. The current center does not serve enough children because it is the victim of inadequate funding.

At the root of this problem is the fact that the resources of capitalist society are incorrectly allocated. Instead of maintaining and expanding needed social services like child care, the federal and state governments allocate funds to serve the interests of a tiny minority of wealthy businessmen and bankers. The sums necessary to expand social services should come from eliminating military expenditures, raising taxes on big industry, and placing a 100 percent tax on all income over $25,000.

The effort to abolish on-campus child care is part of a generalized attempt to roll back the gains of women and oppressed minorities such as Blacks and Chicanos. What is necessary to defend the center is for its parents and staff to join with women's organizations, other student, staff, and faculty groups, and concerned individuals, to wage a massive campaign for child care through education, rallies, picket-lines, and debates.

Child Care Center supporters were handed their biggest setback of the year Thursday when the Registration Fee Committee, in a surprise move, voted narrowly to slice in half its original allocation of student fees to the center for next year.

In a 6-4 vote, the committee agreed to recommend that only $18,600 - down from its first appropriation of $37,000 a month ago - be funneled into the service. According to committee estimates, the funds would cover the facility's operating costs through January 1, 1979.

The move was unusual because no representatives from the Child Care Center were present when the vote was taken and none knew that a proposal different from the one passed four weeks ago was even under consideration.

Mary Wright, director fo the center, said she was "obviously upset" that no one had contacted her or Auxiliary Enterprises head Christian Smith about the veto, before Thursday. She also said she was not consulted about the impact the cut would have on her operation.

C001-01:
Charles E. Young
Chancellor
University of California, Los Angeles

May 23, 1978

Dear Chancellor Young,

Representatives of each of the undersigned groups and other interested students attended the Registration Fee Advisory Committee (Reg Fee) meeting on Wednesday, May 17, 1978. The representatives were there to show support for the full continued funding of the UCLA Child Care Center and the Women's Resource Center and to protest the Reg. Fee Committee's closed door procedures. In addition, hundreds of students attended the April 6, 1978 Reg Fee meeting and the April 21, 1978 Board of Control meeting to support full funding of the Child Care Center 1978-79 budget request which was granted.

We understand that the Reg. Fee Committee is plagued by budgetary concerns and that continual review of programs funded by Reg. Fees is essential for maintaining programs which truely represent what students want and need. We are very much concerned however that the needs of many students are not being represented. These unrepresented students, while not a majority, are a significant and important group on campus and include women, parents and minorities. This group has a demonstrated need for child care and for the unique services provided by the Women's Resource Center. The recent action taken by the Reg. Fee Committee represents a philosophy toward women and minorities which is in sharp contrast to the goals of the University's Affirmative Action Plan.

Specifically, we wish to bring your attention to the following questions:

1) DISCRIMINATION: Is the Reg. Fee Committee responsible for only representing the white, childless, male student? We believe the Reg. Fee recommendations do not represent the needs of women and nontraditional students.

2) IRRESPONSIBILITY AND CLOSED DOOR TACTICS: What justification is there for a body charged with recommending the allocation of student funds to meet behind closed doors and to consider the reduction or elimination of programs without notifying the departments under question? When interested students and child care administrators were present to answer questions, the Child Care budget request (which already included a 9.7% reduction) was approved with a modest .3% further reduction, bringing the total approved request to a 10% decrease from the year before. (The total request is less than .004 of the Total Reg. Fee budget). The matter was then reopened without notification to the Child Care Center and a 50% reduction in funding was approved. Similarly, despite the specific request of the Women's Resource Center Director to be notified when the Reg. Fee Committee would be considering that budget, no notification was made.

3) WOMEN'S RESOURCE CENTER. If the Women's Resource Center is eliminated where will students learn about the changing role of women in today's society? The Women's Resource Center, in addition to providing a comprehensive information and referral service is the only place on campus where women students are able to identify and address their special needs.

4) FINANCIAL AIDS: Why does the Reg Fee Committee believe that the currently inadequate funds available through Financial Aids will be sufficient to meet students child care costs? If the Child Care Center is eliminated in favor of Family Day Care Homes, or if the recommendation that low income student parents be charged fees is acted upon, over $67,000 in State Grant monies ( financial aids) will be forfeited and that burden will be placed on the University's Financial Aid resources.

5) FAMILY DAY CARE PROGRAM: Why does the Reg. Fee Committee assume that Family Day Care Homes can accomodate the 73 children in the Child Care Center and the 400 people on the waiting list? This Program is a necessary and valuable component of the University's Child Care Services and is meeting the needs of many UCLA families. However, it too has a growing waiting list, especially for infants and toddlers where alternatives are virtually unavailable.

6) NEED: The 400 people on the Child Care Center waiting list clearly reflects the great need for this service by many students. The Women's Resource Center addresses the needs of all students on campus by increasing the awareness of the changing role of women and men in today's society, the women's movement, the special needs of women, and the need to improve the status of women.

We urge you to address these pertinent questions and to reject the recommendations of the Reg. Fee Committee. We further urge your support to the Child Care Services Administrative Staff in their efforts to expand the available on-Campus Child Care. The U.C. Campuses at Irvine and Riverside have on-Campus Centers specifically designed and constructed for child care. The campuses at Santa Cruz and San Francisco are in the process of constructing new child care facilities. Next door to the existing UCLA Center is the pest control storage building and parking lot. This space should be designated for a larger child care facility with all of the University's efforts directed toward mobilizing available resources to make adequate campus child care a reality.

Finally, we urge that the Child Care Center be given a three year funding commitment. The continual reevaluation of the existence of the Child Care Center and the Women's Resource Center by non-elected students is both inefficient and costly to all concerned.

More on child care

Editor:

 Chancellor Charles E. Young recently made the decision to eliminate the entire UCLA Child Care Services Department as of September 1, 1978. This decision, which was made without a proper Meet and Confer with the AFSCME-AFL-CIO Union, UCLA Local 2070, effects the jobs of 47 UCLA Staff Employees. It was a flashback to the late sixties—about 40 protestors seated on the lawn in front of the administration building, hugging and kissing, waving posters and singing to the strains of a folk guitar.

One difference was notable, though—about 30 of these latter-day flower children were under five years old and, in addition to chorusing “I’ve Been Working on the Railroad,” they were gathered Aug. 30 to hold a press conference to protest the Sept. 1 closing of the UCLA Child Care Center.

The protest changed to rejoicing, however, as proponents of child care services here announced a final agreement which would keep the center open on an interim basis through Dec. 8. It included the possible implementation of higher parental fees, more parent participation and university assistance in fund-raising.

Chancellor Young, citing lack of funding and contending that child care services are not the university’s responsibility, had announced in June the center’s shut-down and said he would not consider alternatives.

After meeting with Undergraduate President Dean Morehous and Graduate President Robert Dahlstedt in August, however, the chancellor agreed to reconsider his stance.

The new agreement is written as a “letter of understanding,” intended to lead toward the development of “an essentially self-supporting child care program.”

Signed by Vice Chancellor Elwin Svenson, Dahlstedt, Morehous and Convenor of the Parent Council Martin Rothblatt, the agreement includes several elements:

— the Administrative Vice Chancellor will, as of Sept. 1, operate the child care service programs, possibly including modifications such as increased parent participation, revised parental-fee structure and university fund-raising assistance;

— an alternate plan for child care services will be recommended to the chancellor by Nov. 17, 1978, and will be prepared through consultation with members of the administration, faculty, staff, staff union, parents and students;

— Morehous, Dahlstedt, Rothblatt and staff employee and union member Carrie Rothstein-Fisch are responsible for preparing the proposal;

— the agreement will incorporate the chancellor’s earlier stipulations concerning any continuation of child care: an increase in the number of children, substantial reduction in
C022-01:
costs, increased income and, after Dec. 8, possible operation of child care services by an agency other than the campus administration;

— the layoff date of child care service employees set for Sept. 1 was rescinded;

— the committee will write progress reports every three weeks and will receive responses from the chancellor’s office.

If he receives the final proposal by Nov. 17 and finds it acceptable, the chancellor will not charge for the current child care facilities and will give a subsidy from “campus resources” equal to the salary of a full-time program director.

While the children waved signs proclaiming “We Love Our School,” child care proponents declared their general “pleasure” in the final agreement.

“We are very pleased that the proposal has been accepted,” said Child Care Director Mary Wright.

Dahlstedt and Morehous, in a joint statement, said they were committed to the concept of child care here and termed the agreement a “good one.”

President of the local civil servants union Cliff Fried, however, described the agreement as a “partial victory,” and said it would be final only when child care is “part of the university process.”

“We saved 47 jobs,” he added, “but the union is still working to expand the center.”

The union plans to voice their support at the Sept. 22 UC Regents meeting, when two regents will propose a resolution for statewide support for all UC child care centers, according to Fried. “Developing agribusiness is part of the UC’s concern,” he said. “Why not child care?”

Standing on the balcony outside his office, with two microphones under his nose and a television camera grinding away in the background, Vice Chancellor Svenson stated the university’s commitment to “high-quality care” but qualified it with a concern for “the cost.”

The cost per child is “more than is justified,” Svenson said. “We have a commitment to see that the taxpayers’ money is reasonably spent.”

As of spring 1978, the $180,000 budget provided for 74 children. Each space cost more than $2,000—enough to send three students through one year of tuition-free college.

However, child care proponents say the center provides a laboratory for the psychology department here and that the center could be utilized for other research as well.

In addition, not all the money comes directly from taxpayers. The chancellor’s office provided 25 percent of the budget; the registration fee committee voted in spring to cut their funding by 50 percent to $19,000; the ASUCLA Board of Control contributed $42,000; and additional funding came from parent-fee income and the State/Federal Grant for Low Income Families.

In an Aug. 30 letter to UC President David Saxon, Svenson attributed the chancellor’s decision not to close the child care center to the two student presidents’ intervention on behalf of the program.

Morehous said the main purpose of the child care proponents—to have the university accept responsibility for child care services—had “gained quite a bit, since the chancellor was at first not going to accept any responsibility.”

He referred to a portion of the letter of understanding, which says, “The Chancellor expects that child care services will be operated by an agency other than the campus administration after Dec. 8,” but says that the university “does not reject the possibility of continued university operation after Dec. 8.”

Chancellor Young has promised a secure future for UCLA Child Care Services—at least for the next four years and only if they rely partly on non-university funding.

The controversial center, which Young originally planned to close last Sept. 1, will receive a subsidy of up to $24,714 in university funds for the 1979-80 fiscal year. The subsidy will be increased only to cover yearly inflation, Young said.

Other funding sources include California state grants, parental fees and private fund-raising efforts, he added.

The Child Care Study Group—composed of child care staff members, parents and student leaders—developed the proposal to which Young agreed.

The group reduced the original 1978-79 budget request by $158,674. In addition the center will serve 97 children rather than the previous 85.

“Working on the proposal was very worthwhile,” Undergraduate President Dean Morehous said. “It proved the effectiveness of student government.”

And Young agreed, “I believe that the parents and student government officers interested in continuing the child care program have done yeoman’s service. The proposal they submitted to me is an improvement in every way over the previous program.”

But the chancellor warned that any deficits in the program must be met by reducing expenses or by finding additional non-university funding. Young said failure to cover any year’s deficit in the following fiscal year would result in the program’s closure.

Although child care services will continue using their current structure, Young also said any improvements in the facilities will not be paid for by the university.

This qualified support is a turn-about from Young’s summer memo that “the university administration will not, under any circumstances, have any direct responsibility for the provision or conduct of child care services on this campus.”

At that time, the campus subsidy per child—the most disputed statistic—was $1,319. The revised plan calls for $255 per child.

After submitting the proposal earlier, Child Care Services Director, Carrie Rothstein-Fisch said, “I am very pleased, considering the wide range of interests that had to be considered to make the proposal go.”

The four-year commitment will give her time for fund-raising and grant-writing, she added. Previously, because the center came up for re-evaluation every year with its funding requests, the administrative director “had to direct 80 percent of her time just to keeping the center open,” Rothstein-Fisch said.

C205-01:
Get the facts straight on Fernald

By Linda Taylor

Four points made by the campus administration in the Bruin article and in the formal letter announcing the closing of Fernald warrant some rebuttal. The Administration claims: • A six year review process was undertaken. This suggests that the decision to close ' Fernald was based on extensive reviews and recommendations made by the reviewers. The actual facts are: it was only last year that the administration arranged for formal reviews. Two were carried out. One was done by a team of two visiting psychologists who made a one day site visit to Fernald; the other was a cursory review done by four UCLA faculty members who spent a dozen or so hours - including one 2-hour visit to Fernald.

Neither committee recommended closing the facility. In fact, one of the reports stated that the research program at Fernald "is a serious and extensive program and represents a point of view distinctive in the field of learning disabilities..... Fernald (also) has been used in the past two years as a research site by undergraduates, graduate students, and some faculty. Each has been a discreté study..apparently meeting the purposes of the individual investigator." The reviewers' major recommendation was to plan ways to lexpand Fernald's use as a clinical training and research facility. • Funds provided by the state are to be redirected "toward a coherent program of graduate training and research in childhood disabilities." This suggests l) that there are considerable funds to be redirected, 2) there is not a coherent research and training program, 3) plans for a new and coherent program have been formulated, and 4) the proposed focus on childhood disabilities will encompass the type of work being terminated.

The facts are as follows: Of Fernald's current operating budget (approximately $650,000), state funds constitute less than $100,000 or about 1/5. It is these funds that are to be redirected, and in terms of personnel, this means about one staff. psychologist, one parttime research associate, and a clerktypist. This will not underwrite very much research and training - less than currently is being carried out at Fernald - and certainly will not allow for establishment of a major center for research and training. As last year's reviewers indicated, Fernald has been evolving a very, coberent and distinetive research and training program and has provided research opportunities for others on campus. (And there is an ample set of publications to document the fact.) While the idea of evolving a center has been suggested at a couple of meetings in the last year, no specific plans have been formulated. Thus, there is absolutely no guarantee that anything of substance will evolve. (And it should be noted that when the idea was raised, it was discussed in terms of such a center evolving within the context of Fernald.) Not only is there no guarantee that the center will become a reality, there seems little doubt that whatever arises will not have the capability of pursuing the type of research and develópment on comprehensive interventions for major learning problems that has been a central focus of the Fernald laboratory's ef- .

forts. (The chances are that the focus would be on such childhood„disorders as hyperactivity, mental retardation, and autism and would not involve comprehensive interventions to improve learning disabilities.) • Loss of Fernald is no problem because it is only a school and there are plenty of other schools around who do the same thing. This suggest that Fernald is simply a school and the research and training related to the school facets of Fernald are unimportant and easily replaced. (Using such suggestions as arguments for closing Fernald are like saying the UCLA hospital should be closed because there are so many other hospitals in the area or that the UCLA campus itself should be closed because there are so many other institutes of higher education in the area.) The actual facts are as follows: Fernald is not a school; it is a laboratory and clinic which offers a wide variety of services to attract clientele to participate in research and training activities. This* clientele has contributed greatly to a significant amount of research and graduate/undergraduate instruction. (There are ample figures to support this fact, and the flood of letters and petitions from clients, university graduate and undergraduate students, and colleagues in the field also testifies to how much the facility has been valued.) While there are, indeed, schools in the area that serve such clientele, they do not do research and training. They are designed to do as well as they can given the current state of knowledge. But the current state of knowledge is far from satisfactorContinued on Page 11*

Fernald

Continued from Page 10 That is why a facility such as Fernald is needed. It is unique in its ability to develop and study comprehensive and innovative intervention approaches designed to revolutionize the ways individuals with learning problems (including learning disabilities) are assessed and taught. • Closure of Fernald has nothing to do with relocation of the child care center. The fact is, various faculty have been told that the Child Care Center will be relocated to the Fernald site. A related question is, if it is true that the closure had nothing to do with the need for immediate relocation of the Child Care Center, why is the administration is such a rush to close Fernald? Usual practice would call for a more gradual phasing out of a facility that has been contributing for 65 years. (Such a gradual phase out also would have reduced the hardships on the many children who have to be relocated, the staff who have abruptly lost their jobs - some after 10-20 years of service, the university students whose training plans have been disrupted, and the researchers whose current studies have been undermined.) We hereby call upon Chancellor Young to publically correct the record with a forthright statement acknowledging that: 1. Fernald has made a contibution with its research and training activities, 2. there are no specific plans and only a very limited commitment to a new research and training center, and 3. the intention is to relocate the Child Care Center to the Fernald site.

If such an acknowledgement is not forthcoming, we call on those who believe in due process and tair play to exert pressure on the administration to be accountable for its actions. And if the actions are as inappropriate as they seem, we hope there will be pressure to have the decision to close Fernald reversed. Taylor is the Assistant Director of Fernald. Editor:

I am writing after reading Cynthia Lopez’s letter entitled “Child Care for Celebrities Only?” (Bruin, May 14).

I am a parent at the UCLA Child Care Center and, having been on the waiting list myself, am sympathetic to Lopez’s feelings. I am also chairperson of the Child Care Services Advisory Board. The board is keenly aware that there are not enough facilities to meet the child care needs of the campus community, and has made a conscious effort to insure that the waiting list and the procedures governing it are meticulously adhered to.

I am not sure, from reading Lopez’s letter, whether or not she is aware that the Center must be essentially self-supporting. In order to do that, while maintaining as many of the 64 spaces as possible for children of UCLA students, we have had to seek support from the UCLA Medical Center and other sources. In receiving this support, we have set aside 10 spaces for priority assignment to Medical Center staff. Another priority assignment system applies to students qualifying for child care financial assistance through a State Department of Education Grant, for which 33 spaces are set aside. Twenty one spaces are left for full-fee paying parents, either faculty, staff or students.

Each of these three categories has it own waiting list, and the same procedure applies to all three: namely, when a space opens, the first eligible applicant in the affected category is accepted. As a member of the UCLA faculty, John Lithgow’s wife was eligible to apply for a full-fee space in the Center, and to accept it when it became available for her child. The same procedure, in other words, was used in her case as in any other.

Because we do have such limited space, we offer assistance in seeking licensed family daycare through the Child Care Services Outreach Program, headed by Judy Bencivengo. Ms. Bencivengo can be reached for service to any member of the UCLA community by phoning 825-8474.

It makes me unhappy to know that someone like Cynthia Lopez is suffering from the lack of good child care. Please understand that we are doing our best to seek more space, and that the space we have is being carefully monitored.

Toby-Ann Cronin
Chairperson
UCLA Child Care Services
Advisory Board
Senior Administrative Analyst,
Neuropsychiatric Institute

Besides the quality of the center, it would be convenient for me to deliver and to pick up my daughter at UCLA. About a year ago, I started calling the Bellagio center every two months to check on my daughter's admission status, and sometimes I drove up and asked in person. Every time I called or visited, the staff responsible for the waiting list was not on site, so I never got an informative, conversational answer from the center regarding how long the wait is. A couple of months ago, I visited again and - you guessed it - the same thing happened. This time, however, the message on my answering machine from the center told me that our daughter was No. 58 on the waiting list. I was really surprised - and disgusted - because about four months ago, I was told she was No. 40 on the waiting list.

Viewpoint

As far as I can tell, the conditions that decide my daughter's position on the waiting list were not any different two months ago from what they were four months ago (my daughter is 2 ½ years old and has been waiting for the 1 ½- to 3-yearold group for more than one year). I cannot speculate what happened. At this point, we have completely given up hope to have our daughter admitted to the UCLA Child Care Center, and have since found another community child care center and enrolled her there. Fortunately, our daughter's current preschool has been great. It seems staff members get "special" treatment here at UCLA. A part of the UCLA Child Care Center is reserved for UCLA faculty members, while UCLA students can receive state tuition assistance and maybe priority for enrolling in the center. For UCLA staff members, we only get the long waiting list and, in my case, the mysterious reverse in our daughter's waiting position. Yet, we may not earn as much as the faculty members and may not have the earning potential that some UCLA students have. To me, all this seems quite depressing, and Viewpoint's wonderful story about child care at UCLA could not cheer me up. Since the report painted such a rosy picture about the child care for UCLA faculty, staff and students, I would challenge you to look at the other side of the situation, to investigate any problems that the UCLA faculty, staff and students may have experienced with child care, and to find any problems that the UCLA Child Care Center might have. Ask yourself some questions: Do UCLA faculty, staff and students have adequate access to child care on campus? Why do members of the UCLA community have to stay for a long time to get in the center? Is the center's admission policy fair to everyone at UCLA? Is the child care expense at UCLA too high for many staff members? When you find some answers to these and other questions, you will start to understand the frustration and pressure that I experienced here at UCLA: Then, you will see "Child care, the UCLA way" a little differently, and hopefully, you will write an article titled "Child care, the other UCLA way."

C008-01:
Child Care Committee praised

After a year of fruitless attempts Editor: to establish a child care center through the "channels", a group of energetic parents, students, and employees have organized a voluntary day care center on their own initiative. The center opened on Monday in the Women's Lounge. About 30 kids of ages varying from six months to pre-school age played together. What had been felt before as a need had been met in fact for those people involved. By the end of the day, parents who had not been previously working with the group were signing up their kids for the rest of the week. Meanwhile, the bureaucratic wheels have been set in motion. The bureaucracy only moves when challenged. The need for a child care center is not any greater now than a year ago. The Child Care Committee last year found that students and employees at UCLA had 2800 children under six years of age. But this committee never got beyond the proposal stage, and of course the Administration, led by Chancellor Young, ignored every proposal.

However, the Administration could not ignore direct action. When the confronted directly, bureaucracy is forced to react. And so it has reacted. The arm of the bureaucracy in this case is ASUCLA. In response to the voluntary child care center, Don Findley, executive director of ASUCLA, has drawn up a proposal offering University facilities for a child care center available by next April. The Administration would agree to donate temporary use of the horticulture building for a three-year experimental period. However, the agreement is not being made between the Administration and the present Child

Care Center; rather it is being hc made between the Administration 8 and the Administration (i.e. betm ween Chancellor Young and ASUCLA ). Chancellor Young has had the arrogance to say that "I am pleased that ASUCLA has volunteered to bring the project to fruition since it is the logical agency to respond to this need of the campus community." The LOGICAL agency! Indeed!!! For Chancellor Young what could be more logical! But what about the present Child Care Center?? What could be a more logical "agency" than those people who are most directly involved in fighting to satisfy their needs? Not only is the Administration trying to ignore the child care center now operating, but it is demanding that this center get out of the Woman's Lounge after Friday without offering it any alternative site. Meanwhile, the child care center it is offering through Findley will not be open until April. Furthermore, it will be limited to 60-80 children. The Administration has not said whose children will be allowed access to this center, nor have they said how it will be staffed.

These details will be worked out by a committee of at least five members, only three of whom will be from the present Child Care Center. Furthermore, the Administration will have veto power over whatever this , committee decides anyway. Despite the machinations of the bureaucracy, the Child Care Committee has already won a victory. This week's experience has brought people together in a common struggle. The daily barriers of alienation have been broken, and the group has won a concession from the Administration. At the same time, lowever, I would hope that the group does not allow the Adninistration to swallow them.

Peter Lowber

Grad, History

Reconsider

Child Care

Editor: An open letter to Chancellor-Young: I am appalled to learn that you have decided to withdraw all' support for the Child Care Center: that you have chosen to support the leisure time activities of a pampered majority and to ignore, with the blithe disregard of the well-situated, the very real needs of hardworking, temporarily disadvantaged (but feepaying) student parents: This is a model center with an excellent reputation in a forward looking field that has become increasingly important in today's world. The existence of the Child Care - Center was an important factor in -my choice to come to UCLA. When graduate from the law school in 1980, I won't need this service any longer but there will be many others like me who will. I urge you to reconsider your position on this issue for the sake of the many individuals and interests who will lose by your , recent decision.

DB Staff Writers

While an advisory committee reconsiders its budget proposal, onethird of the tripartite funding plan for child care services on this campus remains in doubt. Parents find Child Care Center enhances learning

By Alice Gorton

DB Staff Reporter

The ASUCLA Child Care Center sits between the tennis courts and parking lot 1 in what used to be the subtropical horticultural building. Early in the morning parents begin to carry in sleepy-eyed, sometimes still pajama-ed little ones. Pretty soon the area is a natural thriving playgroundhome: infants are napping sideby-side, while the older ones take liberty to the back yard. Everything appears normal, though in fact for the children it is a rather unique experience. Johnny Murphy, a 20-month-old toddler, has spent half his" life enrolled at the Child Care Center. One of his tight buddies is lan Battie, who at 17 months is a veteran of almost a year at the Center. What their parents see of the friendship pleases them, since they feel that lan and Johnny's is a social experience many other childrep never have.

Johnny's. father, Pat Murphy, describes, his son as "very extroverted - not shy and scared like other little kids." Cindy -Battie, lan's mother, laughs at her son's friendliness. "Itake him to the grocery store; and if he sees another child his age he'll go up and talk - but they don't talk back," she said.

Babysitter

Both parents know that the experience of the Child Care Center has enhanced the learning and development of their children. Without the existence of the Center, or if they had not been luckier than most on the waiting list of 400 preschoolers, their alternative would have been a babysitter at home. "It's made a difference in his life, and that's what is most important," Battie said, Bútaside from what these parents see as the special socializing advantages of the Center, it is generally' agreed by evervbody that problems do exist. "The pay is so bad, and there is DB photo by Scoft Brock such a turnover of staff," Battie sympathetically reports; "but the ones who stay at the Center work hard." The children also tend to catch each other's colds and viruses. "If I had one complaint it would be that some parents bring their kids in sick - but after a while the kids build up a certain immunity." Murphy concedes. He admits that with a babysitter there would not be this problem. Single parents like Cindy and Pat who are working towards their degrees are perhaps among the most grateful for the existence of a child care center on campus. Strong sense The spirit which brought the Center into operation three years ago includes a strong sense of community on the university campus.. It is significant to note that when higher education first existed it was for men only. Not just women, but married women and mothers had to demand to be recognized by universities. Prior to the establishment of the ASUCLA child care center there was a movement for child care on campus which included a weeklong sit-in of parents and their small children at Ackerman Union.

Among those active demanding child care on campus in 1970 were Pam and Steve Brier, then expecting their first child. Their daughter Jenny, now three vears old, has been enrolled in the Center since April of 1971. Because -of -her parents' long association, their view of the Center is necessarily complex. While Pam says that the quality of the care is "quite-fine," she and her husband feel that the original vision has not been fulfilled. Steve recalled that in 1970 approximately 2,800 students and• employees at UCLA had expressed a need for child care on campus. while the Center currently provides services for only 131 parents. Yet in spite of the financial and organizational drawbacks the Center has always faced, it has had basic advantages, over the more expensive cost of babysitting and over other child care centers which only accept children at least two years of age. The type of family with greatest need for child care would in be student or low income families with children under two, according to general opinion.

Problems

There are operational problems on the surface that most people are aware of: an underpaid staff with a high turnover rate, families who cannot pay their bills, a long waiting list. and a general need for better facilities. Alison Wileox, Child Care Center administrator, attributes their difficulties to the financial problems that have plagued the center since its inception: the notion that a child care center should be selfsupporting. Only now, according

DB photo by Scott Brock to Wilcox, are people just beginning to realize that such a goal is impossible. In its third year of operation, partly financed by ASUCLA, partly by fees, and at times in the past by government grants, the Center is presently $30,000 in debt and only half way through the fiscal year. Skeptical of ASUCLA financing in the future, Wilcox remarks. "ASUCLA is a business and child care is not - it can't be." She, sees the solution to funding as'coming about only with help from the University. The original demands, the demonstrations in Meyerhoff Park, the parents and small children who participated in the cúlmination week-long sit-in in Ackerman Union, and the planned threat to bring everybody mothers, fathers, babies, supporters — to the Chancellor's office for a confrontation back in early 1971 may yet have to be revived.

Bill to support campus child care passes Assembly, future unsure

By Dave Peden

DB Staff Writer

A bill to support on-campus child care at institutions of higher learning throughout the State has emerged from the California Assembly by a unanimous 62-0 vote but apparently faces an uncertain future in the Senate and at the hands of Governor Reagan. The bill would tie priority of child care services to a parent's academic workload. According to Bond, the requests for changes are going to be accomodated, although "The exact language hasn't been worked out yet."- The measure, AB 4190, was sponsored by Assemblymen John Vasconcellos (D-Santa Clara) and March Fong (Alameda County) at the request of the UC Student Lobby. The Lobby was responsible for much of the original language in the bill.

The bill would allocate $3 million to support up to' 50 campus child care programs. Presently only 19 such operations receive state support, including the ASUCLA Child Care Center on campus. Parent fees AB 4190, in addition to direct funding of child care centers, would change the law regarding parent fees as they are applied to State matching grants. Those child care centers currently receiving state, monies are required to match one-third of their State grant. For example, the ASUCLA Child Care Center received $53,867 in State funds and paid $17,955 back to the State. Child care centers are presently prohibited from using fees charged to parents to make up the matching fund.

Fees charged to parents receiving financial assistance (welfare) must be subtracted from the State monies. The bill would allow centers to collect their parent fees without penalty, and would allow parent fees to be used as the matching funds.

Revisions

The measure has undergone a series of revisions since it was introduced the end of April. One of the most important changes, according to Linda Bond, co-director of the Student Lobby came at the request of Assembly members who wanted availability of campus child care linked directly to a student parent's course load. In other words, a parent with a full academic course load should have a higher priority for child care than a parent taking fewer courses. According to Bond, the requests for changes are going to be accommodated, although "the exact language hasn't been worked out yet." Governor's veto? Throughout the bill's history, fear of veto by the Governor has been apparent. When it was introduced, a spokesman for Vasconcellos said, "The initial (objection will be the amount of money. As it is now, the governor will probably veto it."

Bond concurred with that earlier evaluation. She said, "Governor Reagàn is acting as if Proposition 1 (a * proposition defeated on the Juñe 4 ballot which would have limited the State's spending) had passed. Apparently he's trying to leave a legacy to the people of California." Bond said "word has come down" that the Governor "will not look favorably on new programming." Outlining plans to get (AB) 4190 into law, Bond added, "We've got to convince the Governor of the need to expand. The bill will get people off of welfare and into an educational program which eventually will get them into a permanent job." Lost Federal funds According to Gary Jerome of the budget division of the State Finanee Department, there is no indieation yet of support for AB 4190 in the State administration. Jerome explained that the State originally began support of child care programs to replace lost Federal funding.

Jerome noted, "Right now the whole issue is a policy issue and a money issue. The original State support was established with the understanding that the State would not directly participate. The State now contributes to make up lost Federal revenues, and they aren't, ready to make a decision to inaugurate new funding under a different premise." Direct funding Jerome said there are other foreseeable problems with the measure. "We think the possibility of direct funding of "We think the possibility of direct funding of child care within the University should be examined closely. It seems that would be a more appropriate method of funding.". Jerome also said he doubted that child care centers would be able to futly utilize the increased funding from the child care within the University should be examined closely. Jerome also said that since every $3 provided by the State or the Federal government requires $1 from the child care centers, he doubted that local agencies would be able to provide the necessary revenue. At present both State and federal aid to child care comprise about $850,000 and require over $200,000 in matching funds. ."If 4190 becomes law," he said, "The amount of matching funds will quadruple." Jerome predicted a rise in parent foes or attempts by child care centers to increase the number of children served— if the measure becomes law. "But right now it's likely the bill will be held over for the next State administration to make a policy decision," he cautioned.

Plans approved for temporary child care center

By Joan Weinstein

and John Bergstedt

DB Staff Writers-

Chancellor Charles E. Young, yesterday, approved the general outlines of a plan to convert the old subtropical horticulture building into a temporary child care center. In a meeting last week, ASUCLA offered to act as sponsoring organization for the child care center "from this according to ASUCLA Executive Director point on," Donald Findley. The stipulations were that 1) it was acceptable to the Child Care Committee established by the Chancellor last year and the administration; 2) the duration of the experimental phase would be three years; 3) the project be as self-supporting as possible; 4) the project serve the entire campus community and not just the students and 5) the administration would agree to donate temporary use of the horticulture building for a three year period commencing upon administration approval of a revised proposal, and agree to pay remodeling costs.

"I am pleased that ASUCLA has volunteered to bring the project to fruition since it is a logical ageney to respond to this need of the campus community," Young said. "I have every expectation that the final proposal will be acceptable to all concerned." Last year a number of proposals were made for a child care center, but were frustrated by lack of money or space. Findley told members of an ad hoc Child Care Committee (not the same as the Chancellor's Child Care Committee which was abolished this week) yesterday the facilities (a total of 5,000 square feet) could accomodate approximately 60-80 children. Members of the committee expressed approval of the proposal: "There's no doubt in my mind that this is a tactical victory," Sharon Heath, committee chairman said. "It's a beautiful first step." Findley also said there would be some room for possible expansion with the removal of an adjacent greenhouse to provide space for trailers. "We hope the proposed experimental project will provide the first step toward determining a long range comprehensive plan for a child care and development center for the campus," Young said. "The proposed experimental center cannot serve all who need child care, but we have to start somewhere."

C044-01:
The Need for Child Care

by Cheryl Shaleve

(Editor's note: Shaleve is a Student and has a child in the UCLA Child Care Center). It really isn't arguable that child care is very expensive; no one expected otherwise. But just as the system of welfare in the United States operates exhorbitantly in à never ending uphill battle against administrations which believe it should not and need not exist, so the child care OPINION needs of the American people are fought by many, I expect, of like minds. Whether the administrators at federal, state, county, -child city or university levels like it or not, there is a need for child care that will not diminish and must be met. Fact: men and women with. children work; thousands upon thousands are single parents. Women, especially, finding themselves alone with children, and unskilled, must return to schoolin order to qualify themselves for employment. This is not a luxury. And if the university is to function in service to the community, these people are among those with the greatest need. The many arguments have been stated often enough to have brought child care to the university but the administration continues to resist.

My family is among those privileged few at the UCLA Child Care Center. If the •center should close down, I would be forced to leave school. There are others in a similar position, some of whom are prepared to sue for the. right to child care on this campus. But 1 do not write for us alone. There are hundreds of children of students, staff and faculty on the waiting list for places which are all too few. I suspect there are hundreds more who, upon hearing that over four hundred were already on the list didn't even bother, or were discouraged from even applying. Still, the administration would prefer a new baseball field to any expansion of child care, even in the face of so great a need. •If football tickets are shunned -at half-price specials, why another field? What kind of value system persists here? Is an educated parent less important than baseball, on campus too?

The child care center provides 420 hours a day of service to the UCLA community, 280 hours, or 2/3, of which to the children of students. It cannot be suggested that Reg. Fees is wrong when it claims too few are being served for so much money; it is true. In my opinion, however, the funds should come from the university as part of a recognized need, an integral part of the present day educational needs of the greater student body, as well as a need of faculty and staff members. The center should not face closure, it should expand. This campus needs child care! While it is true that the physical plant at UCLA leaves something to be desired and space is limited, if a baseball field can and is being considered in its stead, then there is room for expanded child care facilities. Beyond this, should not the university, first in developing so many areas of knowledge, develop our knowledge in quality care as well? With the growing need across the nation and so very few experts, particularly in infant and toddler care, isn't this an area where research funds might contribute to furthering our knowledge and optimizing an heretofore hit and miss experience at so vital a time in a child's life? We have a department of education, a department of psychology, a medical center and other related areas which might take advantage of having such a laboratory on campus, yet child care, a fact of modern life though it mày be, is fought when it might instead contribute, when it might be developed and its rewards shared by all.

To those of you who believe in child care; to those of you to whom expanded child care facilities at or through UCLA would be a boon; to those among students, faculty and staff alike for whom child care is a necessity, here or off campus, I say write, call and have your fellows write and call the Chancellor's office today - before the final word comes down, and let the administration know that we want, need and will not acgept an end to child care services at UCLA. Again, it is not Registration Fees that is at fault here but an administration that - came kicking and screaming into child care, to use the Chancellor's words, and continues to oppose it, rendering it unworkable.

We recognize that funds are not unlimited at the university but we also recognize that certain things are given priority over others. We must ask the chancellor to reject Rieg. Fees determination and see that the child care center is given sufficient funds to develop the kind of program needed for the greatest, number of children. Such a program is already being worked on and should not be dismissed out of hand. The need is too great.

UC student lobby wins 'major victory

DB Staff Writer

The UC Student lobby has already won a major victory in the State Legislature, according to the Associated Students Legislative Counsel, Richard Twohy. He said the student lobby had worked to kill a bill in committee that would make it easier for the University to revoke a student's financial aid if he has been involved in a eampus disturbance. Twohy was hired by the Associated Students two months ago to establish the student lobby in Sacramento in order to tell the Legislature about student concerns.

Regents

"Killing the first bill was a real victory, because the bill was quite oppresive," Twohy said. The bill would have eliminated the provision specifying a special hearing board be convened to consider suspension of state scholarships of a student involved in misconduct at a University. Thus, the Administration would have the decision. Twohy said, "Our argument to committee members was not one about due process. Rather, we opposed it because the particular penalty is inherently discriminatory to the poor, as they are the ones recetving státe assistance."

Punishment

"We felt this punishment should remain as difficult to enforce as the law now allows." Twohy added, "Because of the special inequity of this punishment. it seems unjust that administrators should have access to it at all.". The office barely had enough time to generate the support against the bill, and it was defeated last week by a margin of only one vote. Women

Children

Twohy wrote to the committee, "The lack of reasonably inexpensive, properly supervised child-care centers forces poor persons-in particular young mothers— to cancel their dreams for a better education, and deprives the society of the skills and talents they could develop at the University." Child care suit: another side By Paul Worthman and Stephan Brier The Daily Bruin article of April 29 concerning the legal suit filed against the ASUCLA Child Care Center fails to present adequately the reasons for the suit and the legal and political questions involved The issues raised by the suit (some of which are still very much alive, contrary to the assertions of ASUCLA management) date back to the fall of 1973, as the reporter for the Bruin is well aware. The suit was filed because of the refusal of ASUCLA's Executive Director and Board of Control to face their moral and legal fesponsibilities to Child Care Center families under the terms of the State grant for the period before January 1, 1974. The ASUCLA Child Care Center received a grant from the California Department of Education of approximately $57,000 in June, 1972, based upon the fact that 60 per cent of the Center's 75 families were certified past, present or potential welfare recipients under the provisions of Title IVA of the Social Security Act. The purpose of this money was to make it possible for these families to obtain low cost or free child care at the Center by subsidizing their fees.

In December, 1972, the Director of the CCC, received notification of a mandatory sliding fee scale to go into effect on January 1, 1973. At its

January meeting the Center's Board of Governance discussed the implications of the State grant. The Parent-Chairperson of the Board reported that priority in admission would nave to go to potentially-certified families and that the Center's fee schedule would have to be revised by the adoption of a sliding fee schedule. Some parent Board members raised the question of how, under the terms of the grant, child care on campus could be made available to those student, staff, and faculty families who need sueh care but who would not be certifiable welfare families (this is still one of the major issues regarding the expansion of child care facilities on campus).

In reply to a suggestion that the CCC might reject the grant, the Executive Director of ASUCLA responded by pointing out that he saw the grant as à means to reducé the Center's then-$45,000 deficit. It must be pointed out however, that if the grant were used as legally intended - to subsidize the fees of low-income families - it could not affect the Center's income, unless the Center's fee schedule were changed. ASUCLA continued to take the grant without reducing fees for lowincome, certified families or changing its fee schedule.

Education course to stress work in Child Care Center

By Steve Rubin

DB Staff Reporter

Many students today are finding it hard to relate to the theoretical problems involved in classroom discussions, without being able to discover the feeling of relevance acheived by repeated field work, according to Aleta Letwin, former interim director of the ASUCLA Child Care Center. She said this problem is exemplified in the School of Education where students are taught many theories and problems in child development but often are unable to come into direct contact with their • main subject - the child. However this quarter students enrolled in Judith Ramirez's Early Childhood Education course (Education 423-Section 2) will be able to 'come into direct contact with children, through the facilities of the Child Care Center, according to Barbara Spencer, administrative coordinator of the center.

Letwin said the program will be of intrinsic value to students, in that it will enable their classroom discussions tò be based on experience, and will help • the center utilize the tremendous resource of student workers who will come from the classroom ready to test the relevancy of their classroom theories on child development. The center. through its wide range of volunteer helpers and facilities, provides for the full range of needs of children from two months to five years old, Letwin said. These include social needs, intellectual' curiosity, an emotionally stable environment, and physical needs (children being able to flex their muscles in a fascinating environment.) Students enrolled in Education 423, section 2, will be involved in the center's many activities which could be anything from telling a story to changing a diaper. Students will also take trips with the children. These are explorations, according to Letwin, designed to utilize the many resources of the campus community. Last quarter children saw a special showing of Midsummers Night Dream, watched glass blowers in action and fed the fish in the botanical gardens.

Letwin said the new resevoir of talent from the School of Education will help the child care center in three ways: 1) it will provide more consistent hourly participation to furnish the children with greater care; 2) it will give the staff a more professional outlook, there being more volunteers with a child development background, rather than just unskilled helpers; and 3) it will enable the child care center.to.. expand its program, enabling it to provide many • more activities for the children. Students interested in enrolling in the education course should contact Ramirez in Moore Hall 302.

C110-01:
Young supported on child care stand

Editor: Chancellor Young should not try to be subtle with the Child Care Center Committee. He should tell them directly that it is preposterous and unfair for them to expect other students to assume responsibility for their children. The same illogic could lead me to demand that "the University" (meaning all the students) open a Car Care Center for the maintenance of old cars like my own. Aside from the illogic of shifting responsibility for children to people other than the parents, consider one of the budgets the Committee itself has mentioned (DB, Nov. 11): $275,000 • for 122 children. That's $2,254 per child. If all 2800 kids mentioned by the Committee are cared for at that cost, the bill would amount to $6,311,200. This comes to about $210 per UCLA student if the money were from University funds.

If each child is attached to one studentparent, every such parent would be receiving a gift of $2,044 from the childless students. What principle of equity could justify such a scheme? Suppose some rationalization can be conceived for parents not raising their own children. And suppose it is acknowledged that much of the $275,000 (or $6,311,200) may be for long-lasting physical facilities, not just operating costs. And suppose the cost per child falls as more are added so that $6,311,200 is an exaggeration. Granting all these points, it is still not clear why current childless students owe a "debt" not only to present student-parents but also to those who would use the facility in the future. Maybe the Committee should plan a bond issue to finance the physical facilities of the Child Care Emporium they clamor for. Then they could still lobby for diversion of University funds from educational to babysitting purposes. And, hopefully, Chancellor Young would continue to thwart them.

Nyle Kardatzke

Grad, Economics

Child care authority given to University

By Anne Pautler

DB Staff Writer

The long-debated question of who will administer child care on this campus - the University or the Associated Students (ASUCLA) - seems. finally to have been answered. The ASUCLA Board of Control (BOC) voted 8-0-1 yesterday "that the University should administer the UCLA Child Care System." The nearly unanimous vote - only undergraduate president Larry Miles abstained - stood in sharp contrast to the dissension that previously existed on the Board. In two earlier sessions the Board, after hours of discussion, was unable •even to come to a vote. Members balked at approving an administrative configuration that relegated parent, staff and student input to advisory - rather than governing — status.

At both meetings an impasse was reached when two possible configurations were charted on a chalkboard. One diagram showed a governing committee in the direct line of command between the Vice Chancellor for Administration(James Hobson) and the Child Care Center director." The alternative diagram showed an advisory committee positioned off to one side. Perhaps significantly, no attempt was made yesterday to reduce the final configuration to a chalkboärd diagram. The Child Care Policy Committee that the BOC finally agreed upon - includes representatives from funding bodies (the Administration, BOC and the Reg Fees subcommittee) as well as parents, staff, and faculty and one other "expert" member. But the status of the committee is less than clear.

-BOC member Cindy Climenson, asked whether the Committee was advisory or governmental in nature, called it "a synthesis." "That's a fancy dance but I just don't think it works," replied Ed Shaw _(a voting member of BOC as Administration representative). Later in the meeting Barbara Wade, also an Administration representative, went unchallenged when she asserted, "It (the Policy Committee) is not a decision-making committee." The Committee as planned "develops, recommends, and reviews policies." But Vice Chancellor Hobson cañ disapprove its policies for "fiscal unsoundness, and violation of University policies or official standards," and needs only "advice" from the Committee in initiating his own policies.

The decision to turn administration of the Center over to the University was based on a report by child care consultant Luke Fishburn. BOC member Ron Sufrin seemed to sum up the board's feeling that the University would consider the commitment long-term: "Once they got it, they can't get rid of it." A three year funding package - with commitments from Reg Fees and the University as well as BOC — was also recommended in the Fishburn report. The Child Care Policy Committee would be the appropriate body to draft such a funding agreement, in the Board's view. The Board's decisions yesterday define its own position, but it must await the Chancellor's reaction before the actual transfer of child care administration can be accomplished.

C150-01:
Child Care

by Karen DeCrow

(Editor's note; DeCrow is the president of the National Organization of Women (NOW). This letter was sent to Chancellor Chärles Young on October 4). Those of us active in forwarding affirmative action on university campuses are deeply concerned about the récent decision on the part of UCLA to abandon and close a viable, day-care institution and to substitute in its stead, a poorly thought out program of in-home care for youngsters. We hope you will reconsider this decision for several reasons. OPINION First, noi only do we construe day-care on college campuses as meeting the need of individuals on that campus, we also presume an important other function. University campuses are teaching institutions and as such, should demonstrate to the community at large, model programs providing superior•care for young children, teaching others how to provide this care, and finally, to underline in red, the stance that the university is available to and supportive of women as students, staff, and faculty.

The second reason for our hope for reconsideration of the decision on your part is that the out-reach program as described in several circulars is a very poor substitute for a thriving institutional setting for children. By its very concept, an underpaid woman caring for several children in her home without vacation, illness benefits, job security or opportunity for employment betterment is antiethical to the notion of the improvement of women's role in society. That a university should actively support such a system and in fact voluntarily disband a well-functioning institutional setting is to fail to conceive of its role as an educator of the community at large and a proponent of beneficial programs.• The third reason concerns the allocation of university funds.

Financial stringency is not a sufficient explanation for dismembering the child care center. Various programs, including athletics, are funded in the six figures. What is clear, is that the university undervalues the need for more accelerated progress on affirmative action practices and does not fully appreciate its symbolic and teaching role in regard to the welfare of young children in our society. It is our hope that UCLA will reconsider the needs of the campus. and the community at large, and recommit-itself to institutional child care,-demonstrating what child care can and should be.
